evidence: placeOrder looks up products through ProductRepository, builds an Order (the domain checks quantities and duplicates), checks canReserve on every line, then calls reserve/save. This is coordination across aggregates.
transition delegates the state rules to order.advanceTo and calls product.consumeReserved for each line when the order ships. This coordinates two aggregates.
cancel delegates to order.cancel and product.release.
Persistence goes only through the injected ports OrderRepository and ProductRepository. There is no storage, HTTP or framework code.
advance uses the domain's order.nextState() and only raises an error when there is no next state.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: OrderService is an application-layer use-case service. It resolves aggregates through repository ports, coordinates work across the Order and Product aggregates, delegates entity invariants to domain methods, persists through injected ports and returns snapshots. It contains no persistence implementation, HTTP or transport handling, or framework code. The rules it applies directly are use-case coordination across aggregates, which belongs in the application layer. These are the all-or-nothing stock check before reserving, consuming reserved stock when an order ships, and releasing stock on cancel. Per-entity rules stay in the domain: quantity and duplicate checks in the Order constructor, transition rules in advanceTo/cancel/nextState, and stock rules in canReserve/reserve/release/consumeReserved. One small point: the empty-order check in placeOrder could arguably live in the Order constructor. However, it is input validation on the command, which is a normal application-layer job, so it is not a clear misplacement.
